summary: Analyzes the security implications of IPv6 extension headers and options, as well as the operational and interoperability effects of discarding packets that contain them. It gives advice on filtering such packets at transit routers for traffic not addressed to those routers. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some packets carry extra add-on labels. Blocking all of them might break good traffic, but letting all through can be risky. This gives advice on which ones to block.

questions: should i drop ipv6 packets with extension headers
how to filter ipv6 extension headers at routers
which ipv6 headers are safe to block
does filtering extension headers break ipsec
subtitle: When and how to filter IPv6 packets with extension headers

tldr.problem: IPv6 packets with extension headers can slow routers to a crawl or enable attacks, so many operators block them entirely. But that breaks legitimate protocols like IPsec, Mobile IPv6, and DNS.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes each extension header type (hop-by-hop, routing, fragment, ESP, authentication, destination options, mobility, HIP, Shim6) and each option, recommending which ones routers should drop, rate-limit, or permit based on their security risk and operational impact.
tldr.outcome: Operators can now make informed filtering choices that block real threats while allowing protocols that depend on extension headers to work correctly.

today: RFC 9288 remains the current guidance for filtering IPv6 extension headers and options at transit routers. It is widely referenced by operators making IPv6 security policy decisions and by researchers studying IPv6 deployment practices.

sections.title: Introduction and the Extension Header Problem
sections.content:
IPv6 extension headers let packets carry extra information beyond the base IPv6 header. They support core functions like fragmentation and enable security protocols like IPsec. However, processing extension headers can force router CPUs to handle packets slowly instead of fast-pathing them, making extension headers a potential denial-of-service vector.

Studies show widespread dropping of IPv6 extension header packets in the internet. Some drops are intentional operator policy, but some result from outdated or inappropriate filtering rules. This RFC analyzes the security and operational implications of each extension header and option type, providing guidance for transit routers.

The RFC complements RFC 7126 (which covers IPv4 options) and follows a deny-list approach: at transit routers, only block packets with clear negative implications; do not use an accept-list unless necessary at network edges or destinations. The default configuration per RFC 7045 is to allow all standard extension headers.
sections.eli5: IPv6 packets can carry add-ons. Processing them can slow your router down (DoS risk), but blocking all of them breaks email, video calls, and other things. This guide says which add-ons are genuinely risky.

sections.title: IPv6 Extension Headers: Types and Filtering Advice
sections.content:
The RFC covers nine standard IPv6 extension header types, each with different security and compatibility implications.

Hop-by-Hop Options (Proto 0): can be processed slowly and cause DoS. On platforms that handle them on the slow path and lack DoS mitigation, dropping is advised. On fast-path platforms, forwarding is recommended. RPL routers must never drop them or RPL breaks.

Routing Header (Proto 43): Routing Type 0 and Type 1 are deprecated and should be dropped. Type 2 enables Mobile IPv6 and must be permitted. Type 3 (RPL) can be dropped at domain boundaries. Type 4 (Segment Routing) must be permitted in SR domains.

Fragment Header (Proto 44): enables IPv6 fragmentation and reassembly. Should be permitted because blocking breaks DNS and other protocols that need fragmentation, despite fragmentation's known security issues.

Encapsulating Security Payload (Proto 50) and Authentication Header (Proto 51): part of IPsec. Permit them to allow IPsec deployments to function.

Destination Options (Proto 60): carries options for the final destination. Permit them; blocking breaks Mobile IPv6, ILNP, and tunnel encapsulation.

Mobility Header (Proto 135), Host Identity Protocol (Proto 139), and Shim6 (Proto 140): all enable specific protocols and should be permitted. Experimentation headers (Proto 253, 254) may be dropped at operator discretion.

Unknown extension headers (not yet assigned): operators should permit them to avoid blocking future protocols, though monitoring the IANA registry is recommended.
sections.eli5: Different add-ons serve different purposes. Some are old and broken, drop those. Some are safety features (IPsec), keep those. Some you do not recognize yet, let them through so new technologies work.

sections.title: IPv6 Options Within Headers
sections.content:
Extension headers like Hop-by-Hop and Destination Options can carry optional sub-fields (options). Each option has a type code and purpose. The RFC provides filtering advice for 15 option types.

Padding options (Pad1, PadN) should always be permitted; they align fields and do not pose security risks. Router Alert (Type 0x05) flags packets needing special handling and is used by RSVP, multicast, and other signaling protocols; permit based on whether those protocols are deployed.

Tunnel Encapsulation Limit (Type 0x04) should be permitted to avoid breaking tunnels. Quick-Start (Type 0x26) and CALIPSO (Type 0x07) are permitted when those features are needed. Some options like Endpoint Identification (Type 0x8A) and Line-Identification (Type 0x8C) are deprecated and should be dropped.

The RFC recommends that routers provide configurable, per-option filtering so operators can adapt to their environment rather than using an all-or-nothing approach.
sections.eli5: The add-ons can have sub-parts. Some sub-parts are padding (do nothing), some carry safety info (IPsec), some are obsolete (drop). Let routers be picky about which sub-parts they accept.

sections.title: Security Implications and Mitigation
sections.content:
The general security risk of IPv6 extension headers is architectural: processing them can push packets to a router's general-purpose CPU, enabling DoS attacks against the control plane. Some header chains are complex and can cause information-leakage attacks (e.g., via the Fragment Header). However, the RFC notes that the risk is deployment and implementation dependent, not inherent to all headers.

Operators should evaluate the extension header and option handling capabilities of their equipment before choosing filtering policies. Devices that process all headers on the slow path may warrant stricter filtering than devices with fast-path support. The RFC recommends rate-limiting and per-type configuration as middle grounds between permitting everything and dropping all headers.

The advice is conservative: allow legitimate protocols to function while protecting against the most severe attack vectors. It does not prevent more restrictive policies at network edges (e.g., firewalls at enterprise boundaries).
sections.eli5: The danger is work overload, not the add-ons themselves. If a router can handle them quickly, let them through. If not, slow ones down or pick specific dangerous ones to drop.
